GEN.when: Setting: from Creation to the death of Joseph in Egypt (traditionally c. 4000–1600 BCE). Written form: compiled from older traditions, reaching its final shape around the Babylonian Exile (6th–5th c. BCE).
GEN.where: Mesopotamia (Eden, Babel, Ur), Harran, Canaan (Hebron, Bethel, Shechem), and Egypt (Goshen).
GEN.who: A narrator tells the story; God speaks directly to Adam, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. Jerome's title, Genesis, is Greek for 'origin'.
GEN.what: The book of beginnings: creation, the Fall, the Flood, Babel, then the family saga of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. Its theme is the covenant — God choosing one family through whom all nations will be blessed.

EXO.when: Setting: Israel's slavery in Egypt and the escape under Moses, traditionally c. 1446 BCE (or c. 1250 BCE on the later dating). Composition: layered traditions finalised in the Exile.
EXO.where: Goshen in the Nile Delta, Pharaoh's court, the Red Sea, the Sinai wilderness and Mount Sinai.
EXO.who: Moses is the central human voice; God speaks from the burning bush and from Sinai. Aaron speaks for Moses to Pharaoh.
EXO.what: Liberation and law. God rescues Israel through the plagues and the sea, then binds them in covenant at Sinai with the Ten Commandments, and gives instructions for the Tabernacle where he will dwell among them.

LEV.when: Setting: the year Israel camped at Sinai. Its priestly laws were compiled and edited over centuries, largely by the Jerusalem priesthood.
LEV.where: Mount Sinai and the Tabernacle in the camp.
LEV.who: Almost entirely God speaking to Moses (and Aaron), who relays the laws to the people. Little narrative; the death of Aaron's sons (ch. 10) is the exception.
LEV.what: How a holy God can live among a people: sacrifices, priesthood, clean and unclean, the Day of Atonement, and the 'Holiness Code' — 'you shall be holy, for I am holy', and 'love your neighbour as yourself' (19:18).

NUM.when: Setting: the forty years of wilderness wandering, from Sinai to the plains of Moab (traditionally c. 1445–1406 BCE).
NUM.where: Sinai, the wilderness of Paran, Kadesh-barnea, Edom, and the plains of Moab opposite Jericho.
NUM.who: Narrator, with God addressing Moses; the people murmur; Balaam the foreign seer blesses Israel against his will.
NUM.what: Named for two censuses. A generation that refused to enter the land dies in the desert; their children reach its border. Rebellion, the bronze serpent, Balaam's oracles, and the first conquests east of the Jordan.

DEU.when: Setting: the last weeks of Moses' life on the plains of Moab. A version of this 'second law' is widely identified with the scroll found in the Temple under Josiah in 622 BCE.
DEU.where: The plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, in sight of the promised land; Moses dies on Mount Nebo.
DEU.who: Moses speaking — three long farewell sermons in his own voice, recalling the journey and re-stating the law.
DEU.what: Moses' testament: remember, love, obey. Contains the Shema ('Hear, O Israel', 6:4), the blessings and curses, the song of Moses, and his death. Its theology of one God, one sanctuary, and covenant loyalty shapes the histories that follow.

JOS.when: Setting: the conquest and division of Canaan, traditionally c. 1406–1380 BCE. Archaeology suggests a slower, patchier settlement c. 1200 BCE.
JOS.where: Crossing the Jordan at Jericho; Ai, Gibeon, the hill country; the tribal allotments; Shechem for the covenant renewal.
JOS.who: Narrator; God commissions Joshua; Joshua's farewell speeches close the book.
JOS.what: Israel enters the land: Jericho's walls fall, the land is taken and divided by lot among the twelve tribes, and Joshua renews the covenant at Shechem — 'choose this day whom you will serve'.

JDG.when: Setting: between the conquest and the monarchy, c. 1200–1050 BCE. Compiled by the same school that produced Samuel and Kings.
JDG.where: The tribal territories of Canaan — the hill country, Jezreel, Gilead, Philistia.
JDG.who: Narrator; God raises up charismatic 'judges' (deliverers); Deborah sings, Gideon doubts, Samson riddles.
JDG.what: A downward spiral: Israel sins, is oppressed, cries out, is delivered — and forgets again. Deborah and Barak, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson. Refrain: 'In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.'

RUT.when: Setting: 'in the days when the judges ruled' (c. 1100 BCE). Written later, perhaps after the Exile, as a gentle counter-voice on foreigners.
RUT.where: Moab, then Bethlehem in Judah at barley harvest.
RUT.who: Narrator; the dialogue of Naomi, Ruth and Boaz carries the story.
RUT.what: A Moabite widow's loyalty ('whither thou goest, I will go') is rewarded: Ruth marries Boaz and becomes great-grandmother of King David — a foreigner in the Messiah's line (Matthew 1:5).

1SA.when: Setting: c. 1080–1010 BCE, from Samuel's birth to Saul's death. In the Vulgate this is 1 Kings (Regum I).
1SA.where: Shiloh, Ramah, Gibeah, the Valley of Elah, the Judean wilderness, Mount Gilboa.
1SA.who: Narrator; Samuel the prophet-judge; God speaks to Samuel; Saul and David in dialogue.
1SA.what: Israel demands a king. Samuel anoints Saul, who fails; then David, who kills Goliath and flees Saul's jealousy for years in the wilderness. Ends with Saul's death at Gilboa.

2SA.when: Setting: David's reign, c. 1010–970 BCE. Vulgate: 2 Kings (Regum II). The 'court history' (chs. 9–20) is among the oldest prose in the Bible.
2SA.where: Hebron, then Jerusalem — the new capital David captures from the Jebusites.
2SA.who: Narrator; David's own laments and psalms; Nathan the prophet confronts the king.
2SA.what: David unites the kingdom, takes Jerusalem, brings the Ark there and receives the promise of an eternal dynasty (ch. 7). Then his sin with Bathsheba, and the tragic unravelling of his family through Absalom's revolt.

1KI.when: Setting: c. 970–850 BCE, from Solomon to Ahab. Vulgate: 3 Kings (Regum III). Compiled during the Exile, judging each king by Deuteronomy's standard.
1KI.where: Jerusalem and the Temple; after the split, Samaria in the north; Mount Carmel; Mount Horeb.
1KI.who: Narrator; Solomon's prayer at the Temple dedication; the prophets Elijah and Ahijah speaking for God.
1KI.what: Solomon's wisdom, wealth and Temple — then his idolatry. The kingdom splits into Israel (north) and Judah (south). Elijah confronts Ahab and Jezebel and the prophets of Baal, and hears God in the 'still small voice'.

2KI.when: Setting: c. 850–560 BCE, from Elijah's ascension to the fall of Jerusalem and the Exile. Vulgate: 4 Kings (Regum IV).
2KI.where: Samaria and Jerusalem; Assyria's shadow (Nineveh); Babylon at the end.
2KI.who: Narrator; the prophets Elisha and Isaiah; the kings Hezekiah and Josiah in their reforms.
2KI.what: Elisha's miracles; the northern kingdom destroyed by Assyria (722 BCE); Judah's near escape from Sennacherib; Josiah's reform and the finding of the law-book; then Nebuchadnezzar burns Jerusalem and the Temple (586 BCE).

1CH.when: Written after the Exile (c. 400 BCE) as a retelling of Israel's history for the restored community. Setting: Adam to David.
1CH.where: Jerusalem, seen through the eyes of the Temple community.
1CH.who: The Chronicler — a priestly historian; long genealogies, then David's speeches and psalms.
1CH.what: Nine chapters of genealogies from Adam, then David's reign told again, minus his sins, with new emphasis on worship, the Levites, and preparations for the Temple.

2CH.when: Written c. 400 BCE. Setting: Solomon to the decree of Cyrus (970–538 BCE).
2CH.where: Jerusalem and the Temple almost exclusively; the northern kingdom is largely ignored.
2CH.who: The Chronicler; Solomon's Temple prayer; the reforming kings Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah.
2CH.what: Solomon's Temple, then the kings of Judah alone, judged by their faithfulness to the Temple worship. Ends with the Exile and Cyrus's decree of return — the last verse of the Hebrew Bible.

EZR.when: Setting: 538–458 BCE, from Cyrus's edict to Ezra's mission. Vulgate: 1 Esdras.
EZR.where: Babylon, then Jerusalem — rebuilding the Temple (finished 515 BCE).
EZR.who: Narrator, Persian royal decrees quoted in Aramaic, and Ezra's own memoir in the first person.
EZR.what: The exiles return under Zerubbabel and rebuild the Temple despite opposition. Ezra the scribe arrives with the Torah and confronts intermarriage. The community is re-founded on the written Law.

NEH.when: Setting: 445–430 BCE, Nehemiah's governorship under Artaxerxes I. Vulgate: 2 Esdras.
NEH.where: Susa (the Persian court), then Jerusalem and its ruined walls.
NEH.who: Nehemiah's own first-person memoir; Ezra reads the Law aloud to the assembly in chapter 8.
NEH.what: The cupbearer to the king becomes governor of Judah and rebuilds Jerusalem's walls in 52 days. Ezra's public reading of the Torah (ch. 8) marks the birth of Judaism as a religion of the book.

TOB.when: Setting: the Assyrian exile at Nineveh, c. 720 BCE. Written c. 200 BCE, probably in Aramaic; Jerome translated it in a single day, he says, from an Aramaic text.
TOB.where: Nineveh, the road to Media (Ecbatana and Rages), and the river Tigris.
TOB.who: Narrator (Tobit begins in the first person); the angel Raphael in disguise as 'Azarias'.
TOB.what: A pious blind exile's son, Tobias, travels with an angel, catches a fish whose gall will heal his father, and marries Sarah after driving off the demon that killed her seven husbands. A tale of providence, prayer, almsgiving and family love.

JDT.when: Setting: a deliberately scrambled 'Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians' — a parable rather than history. Written c. 150–100 BCE, in the Maccabean spirit.
JDT.where: The hill town of Bethulia, besieged by Holofernes' army, on the road to Jerusalem.
JDT.who: Narrator; Judith's prayers and her bold speeches to the elders and to Holofernes.
JDT.what: A beautiful widow enters the enemy camp, beheads the general Holofernes with his own sword, and saves Israel. A favourite of Renaissance and Baroque painters (Caravaggio, Gentileschi).

EST.when: Setting: the Persian court of Xerxes I (Ahasuerus), c. 480 BCE. Chapters 10:4–16 are the Greek additions Jerome placed at the end, with prayers and the royal edicts.
EST.who: Narrator; Mordecai, Esther and Haman in dialogue; God is never named in the Hebrew text, though the Greek additions supply prayers.
EST.what: A Jewish orphan becomes queen of Persia and, risking her life ('if I perish, I perish'), exposes Haman's plot to exterminate her people. Origin of the feast of Purim.

JOB.when: Setting: a timeless patriarchal age in 'the land of Hus' (Uz), east of Israel. Written perhaps 6th–4th c. BCE; ancient tradition placed Job in the age of the patriarchs.
JOB.where: Uz — Edom or northern Arabia; and, in the prologue, the heavenly court.
JOB.who: A prose narrator frames a poem of speeches: Job, his three friends Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, young Elihu, and finally God speaking from the whirlwind.
JOB.what: Why do the righteous suffer? Job loses everything, refuses his friends' easy answers, demands an audience with God — and receives not an explanation but a vision of creation's vastness. 'I know that my Redeemer liveth' (19:25).

PSA.when: Composed over roughly 1000–300 BCE; many are attributed to David, others to Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon and Moses. Note: the Vulgate numbers Psalms 10–147 one lower than most modern Bibles (e.g. 'The Lord is my shepherd' is Psalm 22 here).
PSA.where: The Temple in Jerusalem, where they were sung; also the wilderness, exile in Babylon (Ps 136), and the pilgrim road (Pss 119–133, the Songs of Ascents).
PSA.who: Israel's prayer book in the first person — David and the Temple singers; laments, thanksgivings, royal psalms, hymns. Jesus and the Church prayed these words.
PSA.what: 150 poems of praise, lament, trust and wisdom, in five 'books'. The Latin Psalter here is the Gallican Psalter, Jerome's revision from the Greek, which the Church sang for 1500 years.

PRO.when: Attributed to Solomon (c. 950 BCE); collected and edited through Hezekiah's reign (ch. 25) and after the Exile.
PRO.where: The royal court and wisdom schools of Jerusalem.
PRO.who: A father instructing his son; Lady Wisdom herself speaking in the streets (chs. 1, 8, 9); Agur and King Lemuel's mother in the last chapters.
PRO.what: Short sayings on how to live well: 'The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.' Chapter 8 pictures Wisdom present with God at creation — a text the Church read of Christ.

ECC.when: Written by 'Qoheleth, son of David, king in Jerusalem' — Solomon by tradition; its Hebrew suggests the Persian or Hellenistic period, c. 300 BCE.
ECC.where: Jerusalem, in the study of a weary sage.
ECC.who: Qoheleth ('the Preacher', Ecclesiastes in Greek) speaks in the first person throughout.
ECC.what: 'Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.' A searching meditation on the limits of wisdom, wealth and pleasure under the sun; 'a time to be born and a time to die'; and the conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments.

SNG.when: Attributed to Solomon; the poetry may date from the 10th to the 3rd century BCE.
SNG.where: Vineyards, gardens and the hills of Judea and Lebanon; Jerusalem.
SNG.who: A bride and bridegroom sing to one another, with a chorus of the 'daughters of Jerusalem'. Jewish and Christian readers heard God and Israel, Christ and the Church, or Christ and the soul.
SNG.what: The Bible's love poem: longing, searching, finding. 'I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine'; 'love is strong as death'.

WIS.when: Written in Greek in Alexandria, c. 50 BCE — the latest book of the Old Testament — in the voice of Solomon.
WIS.where: Alexandria's Jewish community, facing Greek philosophy and Egyptian idolatry.
WIS.who: 'Solomon' addresses the kings of the earth; Wisdom is personified as God's breath and mirror.
WIS.what: Justice and immortality: 'God made not death'; the souls of the just are in the hand of God. Chapters 10–19 retell the Exodus as Wisdom's work. Its language of Wisdom as 'the brightness of eternal light' shaped how the New Testament speaks of Christ.

SIR.when: Written in Hebrew by Jesus ben Sira in Jerusalem c. 180 BCE; translated into Greek by his grandson in Egypt c. 130 BCE. Called Ecclesiasticus — 'the Church's book' — because it was read to catechumens.
SIR.where: Jerusalem, in a scribe's school, shortly before the Maccabean crisis.
SIR.who: Ben Sira himself, a teacher of wisdom, speaks throughout; Wisdom speaks in chapter 24.
SIR.what: Practical wisdom on friendship, speech, money, women, sons, doctors and death, culminating in the 'Praise of the Fathers' (chs. 44–50): 'Let us now praise men of renown.'

ISA.when: Isaiah of Jerusalem prophesied c. 740–700 BCE (chs. 1–39). Chapters 40–55 speak to the exiles in Babylon c. 545 BCE; 56–66 to the returned community. Read as one book in the Vulgate.
ISA.where: Jerusalem under Assyrian threat; Babylon; the restored Zion.
ISA.who: Isaiah speaks for God in the first person ('Thus saith the Lord'); the vision in the Temple (ch. 6); the Suffering Servant songs.
ISA.what: Holiness, judgment and hope: Immanuel (7:14), the child born (9:6), the peaceable kingdom (11), comfort for Jerusalem (40), the Servant who bears our griefs (53), new heavens and new earth (65). The most quoted prophet in the New Testament.

JER.when: Jeremiah prophesied c. 627–580 BCE, from Josiah's reign through the fall of Jerusalem (586 BCE). His scribe Baruch wrote his words down.
JER.where: Anathoth, Jerusalem (the Temple gate, the potter's house, the cistern), then Egypt.
JER.who: Jeremiah, in oracles, sermons and anguished personal 'confessions'; God's word to him; Baruch as scribe.
JER.what: The weeping prophet warns Jerusalem of the coming destruction, is beaten and imprisoned, and watches it fall — yet promises a 'new covenant' written on the heart (31:31–34), and buys a field as a sign of hope.

LAM.when: Written in the immediate aftermath of the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BCE; traditionally by Jeremiah.
LAM.who: A poet mourns in acrostic poems; the city herself speaks as a widow; a suffering man ('I am the man') in chapter 3.
LAM.what: Five dirges over the fallen city: 'How doth the city sit solitary.' Amid the grief, the hinge of hope: 'His mercies are new every morning' (3:22–23). Sung in the Church's liturgy of Holy Week.

BAR.when: Set in Babylon in 582 BCE, in the voice of Jeremiah's scribe Baruch; composed c. 200–100 BCE. Chapter 6 is the 'Letter of Jeremiah' against idols.
BAR.where: Babylon, among the exiles, with a message sent back to Jerusalem.
BAR.who: Baruch; a communal confession; Wisdom's praise; Jerusalem personified; Jeremiah's letter.
BAR.what: Confession of the sin that caused the Exile, a hymn to Wisdom found only in the Law, and consolation for Jerusalem: 'Arise, O Jerusalem, and stand on high.'

EZK.when: Ezekiel prophesied among the exiles in Babylon c. 593–571 BCE, before and after Jerusalem's fall.
EZK.where: Tel-abib by the river Chebar in Babylonia; visions carry him to Jerusalem and to a future Temple.
EZK.who: Ezekiel, priest and prophet, addressed by God as 'son of man'; extraordinary symbolic actions and visions.
EZK.what: The chariot-throne of God (ch. 1), the glory leaving the Temple, the valley of dry bones coming to life (37), and the vision of a restored Temple and land (40–48). God's holiness departs — and returns.

DAN.when: Set in the Babylonian and Persian courts, 605–536 BCE. Chapters 7–12 in their present form address the crisis under Antiochus IV (167–164 BCE). Chapters 3:24–90, 13 and 14 are the Greek additions Jerome kept.
DAN.where: Babylon — the king's court, the fiery furnace, the lions' den; Susa in vision.
DAN.who: Narrator for the court tales (1–6); Daniel in the first person for the visions (7–12); the Song of the Three Young Men in the furnace.
DAN.what: Faithful Jews in a pagan empire: the furnace, the writing on the wall, the lions' den; then apocalyptic visions of four beasts and 'one like a son of man' coming on the clouds (7:13) — the title Jesus took for himself. Susanna and Bel and the Dragon close the book.

HOS.when: Hosea prophesied in the northern kingdom c. 750–722 BCE, its last decades before Assyria.
HOS.who: Hosea, whose marriage to the unfaithful Gomer becomes a living parable; God speaking as a wronged but loving husband and father.
HOS.what: Israel's idolatry as adultery, and God's love that will not let go: 'I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely'; 'I desired mercy, and not sacrifice' (6:6), a verse Jesus quoted twice.

JOL.when: Uncertain — perhaps c. 400 BCE (or the 9th century). Occasioned by a devastating locust plague.
JOL.who: Joel calling the people to fast and repent; God promising the Spirit.
JOL.what: The locusts as the Day of the Lord; 'rend your hearts and not your garments'; then the promise 'I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh' (2:28), which Peter quoted at Pentecost.

AMO.when: Amos prophesied c. 760–750 BCE, in the prosperous reign of Jeroboam II, a generation before Samaria fell.
AMO.where: A shepherd from Tekoa in Judah, preaching at Bethel, the royal shrine of the northern kingdom.
AMO.who: Amos, in oracles and visions; the priest Amaziah tries to silence him.
AMO.what: The first 'writing prophet': social justice as the heart of religion. God rejects worship built on oppression: 'let judgment run down as waters, and justice as a mighty stream' (5:24).

OBA.when: Shortly after 586 BCE, when Edom gloated over Jerusalem's fall.
OBA.where: Edom, the rocky kingdom south-east of the Dead Sea (Petra).
OBA.who: Obadiah, in a single oracle of judgment.
OBA.what: The shortest book of the Old Testament: Edom, brother-nation descended from Esau, will be judged for betraying Jacob; 'the kingdom shall be the Lord's'.

JON.when: Set in the 8th century BCE (2 Kings 14:25 mentions Jonah); written probably after the Exile, c. 500–400 BCE.
JON.where: Joppa, the sea, the belly of the fish, and Nineveh — capital of the Assyrian enemy.
JON.who: Narrator; Jonah's psalm from the fish; God's closing question.
JON.what: A reluctant prophet flees God's call to preach to Israel's enemies, is swallowed by a great fish, preaches — and sulks when Nineveh repents. A comic, profound story of God's mercy on all peoples. Jesus called it the 'sign of Jonah'.

MIC.when: Micah prophesied c. 740–700 BCE, a contemporary of Isaiah.
MIC.where: Moresheth in the Judean lowlands; addressing Samaria and Jerusalem.
MIC.who: Micah, in alternating oracles of doom and hope; God's lawsuit against his people (ch. 6).
MIC.what: Judgment on corrupt rulers, and promise: a ruler from Bethlehem (5:2, quoted at Jesus' birth), swords into ploughshares, and the summary of religion: 'to do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with thy God' (6:8).

NAM.when: Shortly before the fall of Nineveh in 612 BCE.
NAM.where: Nineveh, the Assyrian capital on the Tigris.
NAM.who: Nahum, in a vivid poem of the city's destruction.
NAM.what: Where Jonah showed Nineveh spared, Nahum shows it destroyed: 'Woe to the bloody city!' — divine justice on an empire built on cruelty.

HAB.when: c. 605 BCE, as Babylon rose to power after Carchemish.
HAB.who: Habakkuk questions God directly, and God answers; a closing psalm.
HAB.what: 'How long, O Lord?' Why does God use wicked Babylon to punish Judah? The answer: 'the just shall live by his faith' (2:4) — the verse that lit Paul's and later Luther's theology — and a prayer of trust 'though the fig tree shall not blossom'.

ZEP.when: c. 630 BCE, early in Josiah's reign, before his reform.
ZEP.who: Zephaniah, a descendant of Hezekiah, announcing the Day of the Lord.
ZEP.what: 'Dies irae, dies illa' — the great day of wrath (1:15, source of the medieval hymn); then the survival of a humble remnant and God rejoicing over Zion with singing.

HAG.when: 520 BCE, precisely dated to four months in the second year of Darius.
HAG.where: Jerusalem, amid the unfinished ruins of the Temple.
HAG.who: Haggai to the governor Zerubbabel and high priest Joshua.
HAG.what: 'Is it time for you to dwell in ceiled houses, and this house lie waste?' Haggai rouses the returned exiles to rebuild the Temple, promising its later glory will exceed the first.

ZEC.when: Zechariah's visions date from 520–518 BCE; chapters 9–14 may be later (4th century BCE).
ZEC.where: Jerusalem during the rebuilding of the Temple.
ZEC.who: Zechariah, with an interpreting angel, in eight night visions; later oracles about the coming king.
ZEC.what: Visions of the horsemen, the lampstand, the high priest Joshua accused and cleansed; then the humble king riding on an ass (9:9, fulfilled on Palm Sunday), the thirty pieces of silver, and 'they shall look upon me whom they have pierced'.

MAL.when: c. 450 BCE, in the Persian period, before Ezra and Nehemiah's reforms.
MAL.who: 'Malachi' ('my messenger') in a series of disputations: God asks, the people object, God answers.
MAL.what: Half-hearted worship, broken marriages, withheld tithes — and the promise of a messenger who will prepare the way, and of Elijah's return before 'the great and dreadful day of the Lord'. The last words of the Old Testament.

1MA.when: Covers 175–134 BCE; written in Hebrew c. 100 BCE, in the style of the books of Kings.
1MA.where: Jerusalem, Modein, the Judean hills; the Seleucid empire (Antioch).
1MA.who: A sober historian; the speeches of Mattathias and Judas Maccabeus.
1MA.what: Antiochus IV desecrates the Temple; the priest Mattathias and his sons — Judas 'the Hammer', Jonathan, Simon — fight for freedom, rededicate the Temple (Hanukkah), and found the Hasmonean dynasty.

2MA.when: Covers 180–161 BCE; a Greek abridgement of Jason of Cyrene's history, c. 124 BCE.
2MA.who: A dramatic Greek narrator; the martyrs' speeches; Judas Maccabeus.
2MA.what: Not a sequel but a parallel account, focused on the Temple and on martyrdom: the seven brothers and their mother, Eleazar, the resurrection of the dead, and prayer for the dead (12:43–46).
people: The seven brothers and their mother

MAT.when: Events: c. 5 BCE–30 CE. Written c. 80–90 CE, traditionally by the apostle Matthew (Levi), for a Jewish-Christian community, perhaps in Antioch.
MAT.where: Bethlehem, Egypt, Nazareth, Galilee (Capernaum, the mount of the Sermon), Judea, Jerusalem.
MAT.who: The evangelist narrates; Jesus teaches in five great discourses, beginning with the Sermon on the Mount.
MAT.what: Jesus as the Messiah who fulfils the Scriptures — the new Moses. Genealogy, Magi, the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, the parables of the kingdom, Peter's confession, the passion and resurrection, and the Great Commission.

MRK.when: Written c. 65–70 CE in Rome, by tradition from Peter's preaching; the earliest Gospel.
MRK.where: The Jordan, Galilee and the lake, Caesarea Philippi, the road to Jerusalem, Golgotha.
MRK.who: A fast-moving narrator ('immediately…'); Jesus acting more than teaching; the disciples often baffled.
MRK.what: 'The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.' Exorcisms, healings, the storm stilled, the Transfiguration, three predictions of the passion, and a stark crucifixion; the centurion confesses at the cross.

LUK.when: Written c. 80–85 CE by Luke, 'the beloved physician' and Paul's companion, for the Gentile Theophilus; volume one of Luke–Acts.
LUK.where: The Temple in Jerusalem, Nazareth, Bethlehem, Galilee, Samaria, Jericho, Jerusalem, Emmaus.
LUK.who: A careful historian-narrator; Mary's Magnificat, Zechariah's Benedictus, Simeon's Nunc Dimittis; Jesus' parables.
LUK.what: The gospel of mercy and the poor: the Annunciation and Nativity, the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, Zacchaeus, the penitent thief, the road to Emmaus. Women, outcasts and prayer are everywhere.

JHN.when: Written c. 90–100 CE at Ephesus, by tradition from the apostle John, 'the disciple whom Jesus loved'.
JHN.where: The Jordan, Cana, Jerusalem (Temple, pool of Bethesda, Siloam), Samaria (Jacob's well), Bethany, the upper room, Golgotha, the garden tomb, the Sea of Tiberias.
JHN.who: The evangelist, with long discourses by Jesus in his own voice — 'I am the bread of life… the light of the world… the good shepherd… the resurrection and the life.'
JHN.what: 'In the beginning was the Word.' Seven signs, from water into wine to the raising of Lazarus; Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman; the washing of feet and the farewell discourses; the passion as glory; Thomas's confession. Written 'that you may believe'.

ACT.when: Events: 30–62 CE. Written c. 80–85 CE by Luke as the sequel to his Gospel.
ACT.where: Jerusalem, Samaria, Damascus, Antioch, Cyprus, Asia Minor, Philippi, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus, Malta, Rome.
ACT.who: Luke narrates (joining Paul in the 'we' passages); speeches by Peter, Stephen and Paul.
ACT.what: The Spirit at Pentecost, the first community, Stephen's martyrdom, Paul's conversion, Peter and Cornelius, the Council of Jerusalem, Paul's three missionary journeys, his arrest, and his voyage to Rome. The gospel goes 'to the ends of the earth'.

ROM.when: Written c. 57 CE from Corinth, before Paul had visited Rome.
ROM.where: To the house-churches of Rome, Jew and Gentile together.
ROM.who: Paul, dictating to Tertius (16:22), in his most systematic voice.
ROM.what: Justification by faith: all have sinned; all are saved by grace through faith in Christ. Adam and Christ, baptism, the struggle of chapter 7, life in the Spirit and 'nothing can separate us' (ch. 8), Israel's destiny (9–11), and practical love (12–15). Augustine and Luther were converted by this letter.

1CO.where: To the church in Corinth, a wealthy, divided Greek port city Paul founded c. 50 CE.
1CO.who: Paul, answering reports and questions from the Corinthians.
1CO.what: Factions, immorality, lawsuits, marriage, food offered to idols, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts, the hymn to love (ch. 13), and the resurrection (ch. 15): 'If Christ be not risen, your faith is vain.'

2CO.when: Written c. 55–56 CE from Macedonia, after a painful visit and a 'severe letter'.
2CO.where: To Corinth, amid a crisis over Paul's authority.
2CO.who: Paul at his most personal and defensive — 'boasting' of weakness.
2CO.what: Reconciliation, the ministry of the new covenant, 'treasure in earthen vessels', the collection for Jerusalem, and Paul's thorn in the flesh: 'My grace is sufficient for thee.'

GAL.where: To the churches of Galatia in central Asia Minor, unsettled by teachers demanding circumcision.
GAL.who: Paul, angry and urgent, writing 'with my own hand'.
GAL.what: Freedom from the Law: Paul's own story, Abraham justified by faith, 'neither Jew nor Greek… all one in Christ Jesus', the fruit of the Spirit. The 'Magna Carta of Christian liberty'.

EPH.when: Written c. 60–62 CE, traditionally from Paul's Roman imprisonment; perhaps a circular letter.
EPH.where: To Ephesus, the great port of Asia Minor, and its neighbouring churches.
EPH.who: Paul (or a disciple in his name), in exalted, liturgical prose.
EPH.what: The Church as Christ's body and bride, chosen 'before the foundation of the world'; Jew and Gentile made one; household duties; the whole armour of God.

PHP.when: Written c. 60–62 CE from prison (Rome or Ephesus).
PHP.where: To Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia and Paul's first European church.
PHP.who: Paul, joyful in chains, to friends.
PHP.what: 'Rejoice in the Lord always.' The Christ-hymn (2:5–11): he 'emptied himself… and became obedient unto death'; pressing on toward the prize; 'I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me'.

COL.where: To Colossae in the Lycus valley (Asia Minor), a church Paul had not visited, threatened by a syncretistic 'philosophy'.
COL.what: The supremacy of Christ, 'the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature… in him all things hold together' (1:15–20); against angel-worship and asceticism; life 'hid with Christ in God'.

1TH.when: Written c. 50–51 CE from Corinth — probably the oldest book of the New Testament.
1TH.where: To Thessalonica, capital of Macedonia, where Paul had been driven out after a few weeks.
1TH.what: Encouragement to a young persecuted church; the dead in Christ will rise; the Lord will come 'as a thief in the night'; 'pray without ceasing'.

2TH.when: Written c. 51–52 CE, shortly after 1 Thessalonians.
2TH.what: Corrects excitement about the Day of the Lord: the 'man of sin' must first be revealed; keep working — 'if any man will not work, neither let him eat'.

1TI.when: Written c. 63–65 CE (or later by a disciple), after Paul's release from Rome.
1TI.where: To Timothy, Paul's young delegate at Ephesus.
1TI.who: Paul as pastor to a pastor.
1TI.what: Church order: prayer, bishops and deacons, false teachers, widows, elders, wealth. 'Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the chief.'

2TI.when: Written c. 66–67 CE from Paul's final imprisonment in Rome, shortly before his death.
2TI.where: From a Roman prison to Timothy in Ephesus.
2TI.who: Paul's farewell — the most personal of the pastoral letters.
2TI.what: 'I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.' Guard the deposit; all Scripture is inspired; endure hardship.

TIT.where: To Titus, Paul's delegate organising the churches of Crete.
TIT.what: Appointing elders, sound doctrine, good works; 'the grace of God our Saviour hath appeared to all men'; the 'laver of regeneration'.

PHM.when: Written c. 60–62 CE from prison, alongside Colossians.
PHM.where: To Philemon, a Christian householder in Colossae.
PHM.what: One page: Paul sends back the runaway slave Onesimus, now a Christian, asking Philemon to receive him 'not now as a servant, but… a brother'.

HEB.when: Written before 70 CE (the Temple sacrifices are still described in the present), author unknown — 'God alone knows', said Origen. The Vulgate places it after Paul's letters.
HEB.where: To Jewish Christians, perhaps in Rome, tempted to fall back.
HEB.who: An anonymous preacher, a master of the Greek Old Testament, in a 'word of exhortation'.
HEB.what: Christ the great high priest 'after the order of Melchisedech', superior to angels, Moses and the Levitical priests; one sacrifice for all; the roll-call of faith (ch. 11): 'a cloud of witnesses'.

JAS.when: Written c. 45–62 CE by James 'the brother of the Lord', leader of the Jerusalem church.
JAS.where: From Jerusalem 'to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad'.
JAS.who: James, in the style of a wisdom teacher; echoes of the Sermon on the Mount.
JAS.what: Faith that works: trials, the tongue, rich and poor, 'faith without works is dead', anointing the sick, the prayer of a righteous man.

1PE.when: Written c. 62–64 CE from 'Babylon' (Rome), before or during Nero's persecution.
1PE.where: To the 'strangers dispersed' in five provinces of Asia Minor.
1PE.what: Hope amid suffering: born again to a living hope, 'a chosen generation, a royal priesthood', Christ's example, Christ preaching to the spirits in prison, the fiery trial; 'cast all your care upon him'.

2PE.when: Traditionally Peter's testament before his death (c. 65 CE); many scholars date it later, c. 100–125 CE.
2PE.who: Peter, recalling the Transfiguration as an eyewitness.
2PE.what: Growth in virtue, the certainty of the prophetic word, warnings against false teachers, and the delay of the Lord's coming: 'one day with the Lord is as a thousand years'; new heavens and a new earth.

1JN.when: Written c. 90–100 CE at Ephesus, from the circle of the Fourth Gospel.
1JN.where: To the Johannine churches of Asia Minor, after a schism.
1JN.what: 'God is light'; 'God is love'; Jesus come in the flesh; children of God; confess sins; test the spirits; 'perfect love casteth out fear'.

2JN.where: To 'the elect lady and her children' — a local church.
2JN.what: Walk in love; do not receive deceivers who deny Christ come in the flesh.

3JN.where: To Gaius, a faithful host of travelling missionaries.
3JN.what: Praise for Gaius's hospitality; rebuke of the domineering Diotrephes; the shortest book of the Bible.

JUD.when: c. 60–90 CE, by Jude, 'brother of James' (and of the Lord).
JUD.who: Jude, with vivid allusions to Enoch and the Assumption of Moses.
JUD.what: 'Contend earnestly for the faith'; warnings from Sodom, Cain, Balaam and Korah against false teachers; a closing doxology: 'to him that is able to preserve you without sin'.

REV.when: Written c. 95 CE under Domitian, by John, exiled on Patmos. Jerome kept the title Apocalypsis — 'unveiling'.
REV.where: Patmos in the Aegean; letters to seven churches of Asia; visions of heaven, of Babylon (Rome), and of the New Jerusalem.
REV.who: John describes what he saw; Christ speaks to the churches; heavenly choirs sing; an angel guides.
REV.what: Letters to the seven churches, the throne and the Lamb, the seven seals, trumpets and bowls, the woman and the dragon, the beast, Babylon's fall, the marriage supper of the Lamb, the last judgment, and the new heaven and earth: 'Behold, I make all things new.'
people: The woman clothed with the sun
